thread:
Jordan: heads-up — after the kernel-chooser change in canary we saw a series of mem spikes and a few OOMs on long-context runs (8k) for the llama-variant. tail latency +15% in the 99th and a handful of failed requests.
Maria: ugh. repro steps? link to the canary? :eyes:
Jordan: canary: rollout/2026-03-17/chooser-v2. Repro is easy: 8k seq, batch 4, dynamic kv enabled. profiler shows a huge transient allocation hit when we pick Triton FFN + FlashAttn fallback path.
Liam: do you have the nvtx trace or alloc timeline? wondering if allocator fragmentation is the culprit or the kernel path itself.
Jordan: pasted a short trace (trimmed):
```
[profile] time=0.0ms alloc=0MB
[profile] time=1.2ms alloc+reserve=1.5GB (triton
kernel workspace)
[profile] time=1.9ms alloc+reserve=2.9GB (flashattn fallback alloc)
[profile] time=2.1ms peak=3.1GB
[profile] time=2.5ms free->1.0GB
```
Maria: so chooser picks Triton for attention because we optimistically assume fwd-only workspace < flash for current batching heuristic, but when seq=8k the KV growth + Triton staging buffer pushes us over the slab limit.
Ash: that matches a repro I had with mixed DTYPE quant paths — cublaslt path triggers a staging buffer for GEMM which doubles transient mem for certain batch shapes.
Liam: two attack vectors: 1) avoid choosing kernel combos that transiently sum workspace + kv peak > slab_capacity, 2) allow ephemeral host staging for the bump (spill to host pinned memory) as a last-resort to avoid OOMs.
Jordan: agreed. I sketched a quick kernel_selector heuristic:
```
// pseudo
estimate_workspace(kernel, seq, batch) -> bytes
active_kv(seq,batch) -> bytes
if estimate_workspace(primary)+active_kv > slab_budget * 0.9 -> prefer smaller-workspace kernel
else choose primary
```
Maria: also batching: we currently pack by batch_size only. Instead pack by active_kv_bytes bucket so requests with large seq don't combine with medium seq in same microbatch.
Ash: +1. we should add an "active_kv_bytes" feature to the router, and a microbatch cap by bytes, not just tokens.
perfbot: perf graph: https://perf.internal/graphs/selector-canary-2026-03-17 (shows 4 regressions aligned with canary)
Liam: could we add a cheap prereq: if seq>4096 and batch>=2 then hard-fallback to flashattn (if available) because it avoids Triton staging for this model shape.
Jordan: flash isn't always better — our runs show FlashAttn uses less transient workspace but sometimes slower throughput. For latency-critical routes preferring flash makes sense.
Maria: other mitigation: allocator-side proactive reserve: when a request is accepted, pre-reserve a small margin for potential fallback allocations so the runtime doesn't run out mid-kernel.
Ash: we experimented with a 128MB reserve per GPU and that reduced tail OOMs but increased fragmentation; it helped stability but worsened throughput slightly.
Jordan: tradeoff noted. Maybe we can make reserve adaptive by current free contiguous slab and recent fallback frequency.
Liam: also investigate opportunistic reuse of temporary buffers between attention and ffn when scheduling sequential kernels on same stream. We can avoid free/alloc churn by keeping a hot-pool of "ephemeral_workspaces" sized by last-used shapes.
Jordan: good idea. Implementation note: ephemeral pool should be bounded and should prefer reusing exact-aligned buffers to avoid split-slab bookkeeping overhead.
Maria: small experiment plan:
- change kernel_selector to estimate (primary_workspace + fallback_workspace + active_kv) and bias against combos that exceed 90% of slab capacity
- router: add microbatching by active_kv_bytes buckets (configurable thresholds)
- allocator: add adaptive transient reserve (start 64MB, increase if N OOMs in M minutes)
- runtime: implement ephemeral_workspaces hot-pool for sequential kernel reuse
- add canary that enables only the selector change first
Jordan: I'll own the selector change. Liam can do router packing. Ash will prototype ephemeral pool. Maria will own the adaptive reserve + canary orchestration.
Liam: quick profiling note — nvprof slice shows the fallback alloc happens after kernel heuristics run and before early memcpy; so selector must account for fallback path memory BEFORE launching primary kernel.
Jordan: yes — failure mode is: we launch primary kernel which assumes less workspace, then fallback path allocation runs concurrently and races with other in-flight requests causing peak exceed.
Maria: infra-bot — please create a canary with these three flags off by default: selector-v2, microbatch-kv-routing, ephemeral-pool. we'll flip selector-v2 in canary to evaluate reduction in mem spikes.
infra-bot: Created canary rollout/2026-03-18/chooser-v2-kvpack-ephemeral (flags: selector-v2=false, microbatch-kv-routing=false, ephemeral-pool=false). Use feature toggle for gradual ramp.
Jordan: thanks. Action items:
- Jordan: open PR with selector heuristic + unit tests and perf harness (ETA EOD Friday)
- Liam: router change + microbatch tests (ETA next Tue)
- Ash: prototype ephemeral hot-pool as PoC (ETA next Wed)
- Maria: adaptive reserve design doc and canary plan (ETA Monday)
Maria: I'll also add a regression test to ci/perf that runs synthetic 8k-batch combos every night so this doesn't slip again.
Liam: can we add a small smoke check to the release pipeline that runs the kernel_selector estimator on a set of shapes and ensures no selector change increases estimated peak memory for critical shapes?
Jordan: yes — add estimator-based gate in release-checks. If estimator predicts >5% peak increase for any critical shape, block.
Ash: one more note — watch for quantized GEMM fallbacks to cuBLASLt which sometimes allocate big workspace on device for algorithm search. Force deterministic algorithm selection for canary.
Jordan: good catch. I'll add a temporary explicit algorithm pin for quant paths until we have a stable auto-tuner.
Maria: ok team — thanks. let's sync again after initial canary run and perf graphs come in. :thumbsup:
Jordan: replying with nvprof traces + a small harness link: https://git.internal/runtimes/issue/867 - add your logs there.
Liam: ack.
Ash: ack.
